the City Council determined that the titles to all ordinances which appeared on this public

PRESENTATIONS

1.  EMERGENCY HOUSING ASSISTANCE PROGRAM UPDATE – F2M20-33

  At the December 14, 2020 meeting of the City Council, the Council requested staff
  submit an updated housing report identifying Alhambra households assisted, including
  the number of households pending, assistance by district, and household demographics
  as in race and income levels. Deputy City Manager TRAN presented information
  regarding the number of Alhambra applications processed and paid, applications
  disqualified as duplicates, over income, or reemployed, applications in process,
  applications on the waitlist, and applications pending a future lottery drawing, if
  applicable. Staff also provided information regarding the geographic distribution of
  applications processed as well as the race and income levels for the applications
  processed since the onset of the program.

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office: Lewis
  MCCAMMON wrote to report on the number of Alhambra residents that tested positive
  for COVID-19 and the need to protect residents from eviction.

  Discussion: Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER and City Manager BINNQUIST
  discussed the ages of people receiving assistance with respect to other services being
  offered to senior citizens as well as the federal restrictions dictating release of housing
  assistance to residents on a fixed income.

  Action Taken:  City Council received and filed this informational report.

2.  COVID FUNDING REPORT – F2M20-33

  At the December 14, 2020 meeting, the City Council directed staff provide a report of
  funds allocated to the City from federal, state, county or other resources subject to
  COVID-19 response. Assistant City Manager GARCIA presented to the City Council a
  report of the various funds that have been allocated from the federal or state level or
  from other resources as well as potential funds that had yet to be approved/awarded for
  COVID-19 response.

  Discussion: Councilmember MALONEY and Ms. GARCIA further discussed the CRF
  formula and the estimated future funds based on the original CRF funds and Alhambra’s
  percentage in proportion to the monies that were made available to the State of
  California at that time. Mr. MALONEY continued to discuss the probability of receiving
  additional funds and the need to support small businesses. Ms. GARCIA discussed the
  potential unspent funds which may be made available and added that staff would
  continue to monitor the situation.

  Councilmember LEE expressed concern for unfulfilled housing assistance applications in
  light of reduced funding projections and the continuing financial hardships faced by
  applicants. City Manager BINNQUIST clarified eligibility requirements to receive housing
  assistance under the current program as well as potential new guidelines in forthcoming
  programs.

1-11-21
   Action Taken:  City Council received and filed the report on COVID-19 funding from
  federal and state resources.

3.  PRESENTATION FROM THE ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY ON THE
  AREA 3 SUPERFUND SITE – F2M21-16

  At the December 14, 2020 City Council meeting, the Council requested an update on the
  Area 3 Superfund site be placed on the agenda of the next available City Council
  meeting. Additionally, the City Council requested a letter be sent to the governing body
  requesting monitoring of potential toxic vapors at the proposed project site located at
  1000 South Fremont Avenue and the surrounding area due to the site’s proximity to the
  Area 3 Superfund site. Mr. Raymond CHAVIRA, Superfund Project Manager from the
  Environmental Protection Agency made a presentation regarding the Area 3 Superfund
  site, which is on file in the City Clerk’s Office.

  Public Comment:
  1) Eric SUNADA reviewed his work with the San Gabriel Valley Oversight Group since
  2008 to provide independent assessment of contamination data with the assistance
  of the EPA for the sole purpose of informing the people who live and work in the
  area. He referred to a letter from the Coalition for Equitable Development which was
  directed to Council, which contained a list of mitigation recommendations. He
  discussed the fragmented approach in the oversight of vapor intrusion in the area
  and the concerns regarding this approach. He supported Council sending the letter
  to the EPA requesting further monitoring of potential toxic vapors in the neighboring
  residential area.

  2) Alexander DeGOOD, representing ELITE-TRC Alhambra Community LLC, Elite-TRC
  North Parcel LLC, and the Corner Company LLC, spoke as well as submitted a letter
  to Council requesting that Council refrain from sending a letter to the EPA to request
  indoor air monitoring for the project at 1000 S. Fremont. The letter is on file in the
  City Clerk’s Office.

  3) Tracey Egoscue, an attorney serving as environmental counsel for the project at
  1000 S. Fremont, stated that she could address the environmental issues for the
  project during the discussion for Item #20.

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office:

  The following people wrote to support Council requesting monitoring of potential
  toxic vapors at the proposed project site:
  1) Melissa Michelson
  2) Katie Chan
  3) Chris Olson
  4) Sean McMorris

  Discussion: Councilmember MALONEY discussed letters of potential liability for the
  release of hazardous substances from industrious usage which were sent to individual
  property owners as well as the continuing remediation process with Mr. CHAVIRA. They
  continued to discuss the cooperative efforts of the EPA, the Regional Water Board, and
  the property owners and developers.

  3
1-11-21
   Councilmember LEE and Mr. CHAVIRA discussed the various mitigation options to
  minimize long-term health effects and prevent contamination such as site testing, a
  vapor barrier, and pre-occupant indoor testing of new developments.

  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER discussed other superfund sites such as the OII
  landfill site in the city of Monterey Park and the International Extrusion superfund site
  which was under review by the Water Board.

  Councilmember MAZA and Mr. CHAVIRA discussed indoor testing in private homes
  located adjacent to potentially hazardous sites conducted in neighboring cities, the
  outcome of the testing process, the effect on local groundwater sources, soil vapor
  diffusion, as well as mitigation efforts to address threats to individual homes such as soil
  vapor extraction systems at industrial sites. They continued to discuss the remediation
  process.

  Mayor Pérez discussed the history of the site and the concerns of the residents. She
  went on to discuss ways the City may support the efforts of the EPA, the specific areas
  being tested and monitored, and the potential need for indoor testing with Mr. CHAVIRA.
  Ms. Pérez suggested submitting a letter addressed to the Regional Water Board and
  requested that Mr. Chavira return to Council with an updated report in conjunction with
  the Regional Water Board.

  Action Taken:  City Council received and filed the informational presentation from
  Mr. Raymond Chavira, Superfund Project Manager from the Environmental Protection
  Agency and the letter dated January 6, 2021 and attached to the Director of Public
  Works & Utilities’ January 11, 2021 report that was sent requesting monitoring of
  potential toxic vapors at the proposed project site located at 1000 South Fremont and
  the surrounding area.

7.  APPROVE GUIDELINES FOR PREPARING CITY COUNCIL MINUTES – F2M21-20,
  M2M21-2

  At the December 14, 2020 regular meeting of the Alhambra City Council, Mayor Pérez
  requested, and the Council unanimously concurred, that an item regarding transitioning
  to action minutes for City Council meetings be brought back for City Council
  consideration. In 2015, the City Clerks Association of California (CCAC) published its
  Guidelines for Preparing Minutes and recommended municipalities consider adopting
  these guidelines that call for either brief summary or action style minutes. The City has
  used long-form style minutes, as opposed to brief summary or action minutes. Most
  California cities have transitioned from long-form minutes to either brief summary or
  action minutes as the most efficient, succinct, and cost-effective manner for preparing a
  record of City Council action. Auditors, judicial officers, the public, and other
  stakeholders rely on minutes to accurately reflect the final decisions of the body.
  Additionally, streamlining to brief summary or action minutes would reduce the amount
  of staff time spent in minutes preparation. Other cost savings would include the
  reduction in materials (pages, books) used for preserving archival minutes. In the case
  of someone wishing to review the discussion leading up to the Council’s final decision,
  audio/video recordings of the Council’s proceedings, as well as agenda packets, are
  maintained pursuant to the City’s records retention policy.

  Public Comment:  Henry FUNG expressed concern regarding the lack of City
  Council meeting agendas and minutes prior to 2018 available on the city website as well

  6
1-11-21
   as the 10 year retention period for the audio and video recordings of City Council
  meetings. He suggested that given improved data storage that the retention period for
  audio and video recordings change to indefinite.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council approved transitioning to “action” or “brief” summary
  style for the City Council’s official minutes as outlined in the City Clerks Association of
  California (CCAC) Guidelines for Preparing Minutes and directed the City Clerk to
  transition from long-form style minutes to action or brief summary minutes, following the
  CCAC guidelines, for any outstanding minutes not yet completed. Furthermore, City
  Council directed the City Clerk to prepare action minutes, providing a brief summary only
  in those instances where the Clerk deems it appropriate to make the action of the
  Council clearer. (M2M21-2)

  Vote:  Moved:  MALONEY  Seconded: LEE
  Ayes:  LEE, MAZA, MALONEY, PÉREZ
  Noes:  ANDRADE-STADLER

8.  RESOLUTION SUPPORTING THE COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES LA VS. HATE
  (UNITED AGAINST HATE) CAMPAIGN – F2M21-16, R2M21-1

  The purpose of United Against Hate nationwide campaign was to bring together cities,
  school districts, and civic organizations to help foster a network of support and resources
  for communities to respond and prevent hate and promote inclusion and equity for all.
  The initiative began in 2017 and in its third year, the United Against Hate campaign
  helped communities lead meaningful, locally-driven actions and conversations in support
  of working across differences to build stronger communities. The Los Angeles County
  Board of Supervisors was active in promoting efforts supporting the United Against Hate
  campaign. These efforts included engaging community members across the County and
  raising awareness. In addition, the County invited cities to join the conversation. By
  participating in the County’s LA vs. Hate (United Against Hate) campaign, the City made
  a commitment to make everyone feel safe and supported by raising awareness and
  promoting inclusion and equity for all.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council adopted Resolution No. R2M21-1 entitled: A
  Resolution of the Alhambra City Council supporting the County of Los Angeles’ LA vs.
  Hate (United Against Hate) Campaign

  Vote:  Moved:  MALONEY  Seconded: LEE
  Ayes:  LEE, MAZA, MALONEY, PÉREZ

  SAFE CLEAN WATER MUNICIPAL PROGRAM FUND – F2M20-17, O2M21-4782,
  M2M21-8

  Section 3.32.010 of the Alhambra Municipal Code creates and establishes the funds and
  account groups for the conduct and operation of the municipal fiscal affairs of the city
  government, including those funds established by the City Charter. The City would begin
  to receive the Safe Clean Water Municipal Program (SCW) funds from the Los Angeles
  County Flood Control District for Fiscal Year 2019-20. SCW estimated the City would
  receive $860,000 of SCW funds in Fiscal Year 2020-21. The Los Angeles County Flood
  Control District (District) administered the SCW Program for the purpose of funding
  projects to increase stormwater and urban runoff capture as well as reduce stormwater
  and urban runoff pollution in the District. These funds were restricted and may only be
  expended for eligible costs. The creation of Section 3.32.149 for the Safe Clean Water
  Program was necessary to provide better tracking of funds received and related
  expenditures to ensure compliance with program requirements.

  implemented under the program with Director of Public Works/Utilities RAY. Mr. Maloney
  supported the ordinance and the program.

  In 2015, the State of California adopted Assembly Bill 1236 (2015, Chiu, Codified as
  Government Code Section 65850.7), which required local jurisdictions to adopt an
  ordinance to create an expedited, streamlined permitting process for electric vehicle
  charging stations. An electric vehicle charging station is any level of electric vehicle
  supply equipment station which delivers electricity from a source outside an electric
  vehicle into a plug-in electric vehicle. AB 1236 may refer to the recommendations in the
  most current version of the “Plug-In Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Permitting Checklist”
  of the “Zero-Emission Vehicles in California: Community Readiness Guidebook”
  published by the Governor’s Office of Planning and Research.

  163

  This was the time and place set by Notice No. N2M20-163 for the City Council to hold a
  public hearing to consider applications filed by ELITE-TRC Alhambra Community LLC,
  Elite-TRC North Parcel LLC; The Corner Company, LLC for Vesting Tentative Tract Map
  TT 74194, Residential Planned Development Permit RP-17-7, Conditional Use Permit
  CU-17-9 and Development Agreement for the Development of the Proposed Villages at
  the Alhambra Project (Project). Principal Planner LAM delivered a staff report. The
  Project covered portions of a 38.38-acre site bounded by Fremont Avenue (west),
  Mission Road (south), Date Avenue (east), and Orange Street (north) in the City of
  Alhambra. The Project site was located in the PO (Professional Office) zone. The
  applicant requested approval of a Vesting Tentative Tract Map, Residential Planned
  Development Permit, Conditional Use Permit and Development Agreement for the
  development of the Project, as well as certification of an Environmental Impact Report
  (EIR) and adoption of a Statement of Overriding Considerations (SOC). If approved, the
  Project would retain 902,001 square feet of existing office space and would repurpose
  10,145 square feet of existing office space as Residential Amenity space. Also, the
  Project would retain a 50,000 square-foot LA Fitness health club, but would replace
  existing surface parking areas, warehouse/storage/maintenance buildings, and a vacant
  office building with a new multi-family residential development. The Project was originally
  submitted as a 1,061-unit development with 516 new, for-sale, residential dwelling units
  in five-story stacked flat and townhome configurations and 545 new rental apartments in
  five-story stacked flat configurations. Through the Planning Commission process, the
  Applicant modified the Project and reduced the number of proposed units to 839 (294
  for-sale, 545 rentals). Up to 4,347 new parking spaces would be provided to
  accommodate all of the uses, existing and new. The portions of the Project site slated for
  new development are designed in four Plan Areas: North Plan Area, East Plan Area,
  South Plan Area, and Corner Plan Area. The details of each Plan Area are discussed in
  further detail in the Residential Planned Development Section of this Analysis. The
  Project also proposed a reduction in the number of required parking spaces which was
  discussed in further detail in the Parking Section of this Analysis. It was the intent of the
  Applicant to develop the Project in phases. In furtherance of this, the Applicant proposed
  a Development Agreement for the Project.

  14
1-11-21
   Between July 20, 2020 and November 16, 2020, the Planning Commission conducted
  nine (9) public hearings in considering the proposed The Villages at The Alhambra
  Project. At the September 21, 2020 Planning Commission meeting, the public comments
  portion of the public hearing closed with a total of 36 members of the public having
  spoken and 339 written comments read into the record. At the October 5, 2020 Planning
  Commission meeting each of the Planning Commissioners were able to ask technical
  questions and express their thoughts and concerns. At the heart of the Planning
  Commission’s concerns were five (5) issues pertaining to Project Density,
  Affordability/Inclusionary  Housing,  Community  Benefits/Open  Space,
  Traffic/Transportation, and Health/Site Contamination. At the November 2, 2020
  Planning Commission meeting the Applicant returned to the Commission a Project with
  three (3) modifications: 1) The total number of units was reduced from 1,061 (516 for-
  sale, 545 rentals) to 839 (294 for-sale, 545 rentals); 2) The number of affordable housing
  units was increased from 55 units to 84 units; and 3) The Applicant decided to redesign
  the open space area in the North Plan Area to create a community park accessible to
  everyone, including the public. The Planning Commission was of the opinion these
  modifications were not sufficient and by a vote of 7-3, directed staff to return to the
  Commission at the November 16, 2020 meeting, with a Resolution recommending the
  City Council deny the proposed Project. At the November 16, 2020 Planning
  Commission meeting, by a vote of 7-1, the Planning Commission adopted Resolution
  No. 20-20 recommending the City Council deny the proposed Project.

  Megan MOLOUGHNEY, Senior Development Manager for The Ratkovich Company,
  and several consultants delivered an overview presentation of The Villages at the
  Alhambra project. The presentation is on file in the City Clerk’s office. The other
  presenters included architect Winston Chang of Next Architecture, EIR consultant Rob
  Carnachan from CAJA Environmental, Traffic consultant Sri Chakravarthy of Kimley-
  Horn, housing and economic development consultant Paul Silvern of HRA Advisors, and
  Wayne Ratkovich, founder of The Ratkovich Company.
